# Cycle 0001 Insight

## Cohort outcome

This founding cohort probed three independent axes against baseline: where
promoted items land (v001), how aggressively warm keys earn promotion (v002),
and how fat each `Item` is on the metadata axis (v003). All three entered the
Winners, but for different reasons — the two unambiguous wins (v001, v003) paid
off on latency and/or size with no regression, while the aggressive-promotion
variant (v002) was a controlled loss on hit-rate that bought only an incidental
latency gain.

## Patterns

- Per-op-time was the easy, repeatable win this cycle: every variant trimmed
  latency, and in each case the cause was removing hidden hot-path cost — an
  O(n) front-shift (v001), a candidate-scan branch (v002), or an
  `Instant::now()` syscall (v003) — rather than algorithmic cleverness.
- Hit-rate behaved as a balance, not a free lunch. Steering *where* a hot key
  lands (v001) lifted retention, but simply promoting *more* keys (v002) flooded
  the probing tier and evicted otherwise-resident keys. The hottest-only gate
  was load-bearing, not dead weight.
- The active eval policy is `ClassicLRU`, which is purely positional. v003
  exposed that the baseline `Item` carried `timestamp` and a word-sized LFU
  counter that the exercised policy never reads — pure overhead on size and
  latency.

## Open questions

- v001 (MRU promotion) and v002 (ungated promotion) move the same lever in
  tension — does a *gated* promotion that lands at MRU (v001's position with
  v002's filter retained) compound the hit-rate gain, or do the effects cancel?
- Is there a middle promotion gate between "single hottest" and "every
  re-access" that widens the protected set without churning the probing tier?
- Since `ClassicLRU` ignores recency/frequency metadata, how much more `Item`
  footprint is dead weight under the current eval config?

## Continuation

Pursue v001's MRU-promotion direction and treat v003's metadata trimming as a
near-free baseline to build on; both are safe foundations. Drop the
unconditional-promotion idea (v002) as-is — the hottest-only gate matters — but
keep its insight that promotion volume must be filtered. Next cycle should test
combining MRU placement with a tunable promotion gate, and explore further
`Item` slimming given the positional-only eval policy.

# Cycle 0002 Insight

## Cohort outcome

This cohort cashed in cycle-0001's two safe directions and answered its
open question. All three variants entered the Winners: two pushed `Item`
footprint to its floor (v001 stacks v003's slim `Item` onto v001's MRU
promotion; v002 deletes the last metadata field outright), and one
(v003) widened the promotion gate from "single hottest" to a proportional
top-quarter window, lifting hit-rate above the v001 incumbent without
re-introducing v002-cycle-0001's churn.

## Patterns

- Placement and footprint proved genuinely orthogonal: porting the slim
  `Item` onto the MRU-promotion winner added both wins (smaller entries,
  faster ops) while leaving hit-rate untouched, confirming cycle-0001's
  bet that the two axes don't trade against each other.
- Metadata slimming bottomed out this cycle. Once `timestamp` was gone,
  the lone frequency counter was the only thing padding `Item<u64,u64>`
  past its bare key+value core; deleting it collapsed the alignment
  padding for free because the active positional `ClassicLRU` never read
  the field. There is little metadata left to remove.
- The middle-ground promotion gate worked, but the gain was small — the
  bulk of protectable warm mass on this trace already sits near the MRU
  head, so a quarter-window captures most of what the tight gate missed.
  Widening also shortened target buckets, so latency improved alongside
  hit-rate rather than trading against it.

## Open questions

- Does combining the slim `Item` (H01/H02 footprint floor) with the
  top-quarter promotion gate (v003) compound cleanly, or does the
  shorter-bucket effect of the wider gate change the placement calculus?
- The quarter-window gain was small — is there a better-shaped gate
  (different fraction, or recency-weighted rather than positional) that
  reaches the warm keys the window still misses, or is the trace's
  protectable mass simply near-exhausted?
- With `Item` now at its byte floor, where does the next size win come
  from — bucket/segment structure rather than per-entry layout?

## Continuation

Carry forward the merged best: slim `Item` at its 16-byte floor plus the
top-quarter promotion gate, as the new baseline to beat. Treat further
per-entry metadata trimming as exhausted — pivot the size axis to
container/segment structure instead. On hit-rate, the positional window
is near diminishing returns; next cycle should test gate *shape* (varying
the fraction or trying a non-positional weighting) rather than just gate
*width*, and probe whether placement and the wider gate still stack when
applied together.

# Cycle 0003 Insight

## Cohort outcome

All three variants forked from the cycle-0002 slim+MRU base and probed the
promotion-gate / hot-path axis: a wider positional window (v001), a
frequency-driven gate spending the free `lfu_counter` (v002), and a pure
branch-reorder latency play (v003). All three entered the Winners, but this
was a cohort of near-null results — every change landed within or below the
trace/measurement noise floor, with no clean compounding win among them.

## Patterns

- The promotion-gate axis has saturated on this trace. Widening the gate
  (v001) and switching it from positional to frequency (v002) each nudged
  hit-rate up only marginally, because MRU placement (`InsertPosition::Back`)
  already captures the warm mass either lever would protect — gate shape and
  MRU placement are substitutes, not additive. This directly answers cycle
  0002's open questions 1 and 2: protectable warmth is near-exhausted.
- Touching the hot `get` path to chase hit-rate carries real latency cost
  with little payoff: both the wider gate's promotion cascade (v001) and the
  per-hit counter read-modify-write (v002) raised p50 for a hit-rate gain
  indistinguishable from noise.
- Micro-latency reorders are below this harness's resolution. v003's branch
  reorder strictly removes a scan per hit yet moved latency the wrong way —
  and even `put`, which the change can't touch, regressed — confirming the
  saving is swamped by variance.

## Open questions

- With both placement and gate shape exhausted on hit-rate, is there any
  remaining lever on this trace that isn't noise-limited, or is hit-rate
  fully tapped?
- Since the harness can't resolve single-scan-per-hit savings, what
  granularity of structural change *is* large enough to measure?

## Continuation

Stop tuning the promotion gate and hot-path probe order — that axis is
saturated and its effects sit below the noise floor; further gate-shape or
reorder variants are not worth a slot. Pivot decisively to the
container/segment structure for the next real win (the size axis flagged in
cycle 0002), and size any future latency hypothesis to clear the measurement
noise floor rather than chasing per-hit micro-savings.

# Cycle 0004 Insight

## Cohort outcome

Acting on cycle-0003's mandate, this cohort abandoned gate tuning and
attacked three structurally distinct levers: a segment-owned side table to
break the size/hit-rate trade (v001), hot-path devirtualization of the
eviction policy (v002), and raised set-associativity for hit-rate (v003).
All three entered the Winners, and together they resolved the cycle's open
questions — one reaching the long-sought Pareto corner, one establishing what
the harness can actually measure, and one cleanly falsifying a miss-class
hypothesis.

## Patterns

- The container/segment pivot paid off where per-entry tuning could not.
  Relocating the promotion-heat signal out of `Item` into a segment-side map
  (v001) finally occupied the open Pareto corner — the incumbent's best
  hit-rate held bit-for-bit AT the metadata floor that the counter-carrying
  parent could not reach. The structure-vs-layout split flagged since cycle
  0002 was the right frame.
- Structural latency change *is* resolvable; micro-reorders were not.
  Devirtualizing the trait-object call and enabling remove+push inlining
  (v002) moved median/get-tail latency above the noise floor that swallowed
  cycle-0003's branch reorder, directly answering "what granularity is
  detectable."
- Hit-rate is now firmly capacity/compulsory-bound, not conflict-bound.
  Widening the neighborhood to 3-wide (v003) left hit-rate bit-for-bit
  unchanged, falsifying the conflict-miss hypothesis and closing
  associativity as a dead lever — alongside the already-saturated gate and
  placement axes.
- Side tables trade tail latency for size: v001's free struct read became a
  hash-and-probe, pushing p99 up. Relocation is not a free substitute.

## Open questions

- With placement, gate shape, and associativity all exhausted on hit-rate,
  is any remaining lever capable of moving it, or is it fully capped by the
  trace's compulsory/capacity mass?
- Can the v002 devirtualization win and the v001 side-table relocation be
  combined, or does the side-table's added hot-path hashing eat the
  devirtualization latency gain?
- Are there further structural latency wins of v002's magnitude (allocation
  strategy, bucket layout), and can any reduce p99 rather than just p50?

## Continuation

Carry forward v002's devirtualized hot path as the new latency baseline — it
is the clearest, harness-resolvable win available. Treat hit-rate as capped:
stop spending slots on gate, placement, or associativity variants. For size,
v001's side-table reaches the Pareto corner but at a tail-latency cost worth
revisiting; next cycle should test whether v002's latency win and v001's size
win stack, and keep size/latency hypotheses sized to clear the noise floor.

# Cycle 0005 Insight

## Cohort outcome

This cohort tried to bank the cycle-0004 wins by composition and to close
the last open hit-rate class: stacking v002's devirtualized hot path onto
v001's side-table parent (v001), monomorphizing the outer Bucket trait
object one layer further (v002), and adding a frequency-aware ghost-list
admission lever (v003). All three entered the Winners, but the cohort was a
clean sweep of confirmatory negatives — every promised stack either failed
to compose or regressed latency, and the new lever moved nothing.

## Patterns

- The two cycle-0004 Pareto wins are substitutive on a shared hot path, not
  additive. Porting devirtualization onto the side-table parent left get-p50
  pinned at the parent's floor, because the `target_heat` hash probe — not
  the vtable dispatch — is what bounds that variant's latency. You cannot
  collect both speedups while the side-table hash sits on the same get path.
- Structural devirtualization only pays when it removes indirection without
  fattening layout. Collapsing the *outer* Bucket trait object replaced a
  compact heap pointer per slot with a fat inline struct, widening the `Vec`
  stride and regressing every per-op metric — the inverse of the inner-policy
  win. The heap pointer was buying locality; removing it cost more than the
  saved dispatch.
- Hit-rate is now confirmed capacity/compulsory-capped against every class.
  The admission/frequency lever — the one untried family — left hit-rate
  bit-for-bit at the recency-only ceiling, buying only put latency from its
  ghost bookkeeping. Placement, gate, associativity, and now admission are
  all exhausted.

## Open questions

- With composition shown to be substitutive on the shared get path, is there
  a hot-path layout where the side-table relocation and the devirtualization
  stop competing — or is the metadata-floor corner and the latency floor
  simply mutually exclusive?
- Every remaining latency lever this cycle either fattened layout or added
  bookkeeping. Is there a structural change that removes indirection while
  *preserving or improving* locality, or has latency also saturated?

## Continuation

Treat hit-rate as fully closed — admission was the last class and it moved
nothing; spend no further slots probing it. Stop attempting to stack the
cycle-0004 size and latency winners on a single hot path: they are
substitutive, and outer-layer monomorphization regresses locality. The two
banked corners (v002 devirtualized latency baseline, v001 side-table size
corner) stand as the frontier; next cycle should look for a latency change
that improves locality rather than adds indirection or inline bloat, and
otherwise accept the frontier may be converged.

# Cycle 0006 Insight

## Cohort outcome

All three variants forked from the cycle-0005 v001 side-table parent and
attacked the same documented bottleneck — the `target_heat` side-table probe
that bounds that variant's get latency — by three routes: swap SipHash for a
trivial `u64` hasher (v001), pre-reserve capacity to kill rehash spikes
(v002), and replace the hash with a position-aligned per-bucket `Vec<u8>`
(v003). All three entered the Winners, but only v001 was a clean win: it cut
all four op-latency metrics with no regression and broke below the parent's
get-p50 floor at the metadata corner — proving cycle 0005's "frontier may be
converged" call was premature.

## Patterns

- The side-table cost was the *hasher*, not the hash structure. The
  bottleneck cycle 0005 pinned on this probe was SipHash overkill on
  integer keys; removing the keyed permutation while keeping the `HashMap`,
  the gate decisions, and the layout byte-for-byte moved get-p50 below the
  parent floor for free. This is the locality-preserving latency win the
  prior cycle's open question asked for — and it lived inside the existing
  structure, not in a new one.
- Tail and median latency on this probe have separable causes. The hasher
  swap (v001) moved p50 and both tails together; capacity pre-reservation
  (v002) cut only the get p99 rehash spike and left put p99 untouched —
  confirming put's tail is gated by a different mechanism the side table
  can't reach. Median is hasher-bound; the get tail is rehash-bound; the put
  tail is neither.
- Eliminating the hash entirely backfired (v003): a position-aligned
  parallel `Vec<u8>` must ride along with its item through every ClassicLRU
  remove+push, paying an O(n) element shift on *every* hit versus the
  parent's target-only hashed probe — slower, not faster, and the alignment
  also failed to reproduce the promotion-gate semantics exactly, nicking
  hit-rate. The hash was never the bottleneck; the *keyed permutation* on top
  of it was.

## Open questions

- v001 (hasher swap) and v002 (capacity reservation) are orthogonal by
  construction — one hits median, the other the get tail. Do they compose
  into a single variant that wins both, unlike the substitutive stacks of
  cycle 0005?
- The put p99 tail resisted every lever this cycle. What mechanism on the put
  path bounds it, and is it reachable at all?

## Continuation

The frontier was not converged: trivializing the `u64` hasher on the
side-table probe is the new latency baseline at the metadata corner — carry
it forward. Because v001 and v002 target disjoint causes (median hasher cost
vs. get-tail rehash cost), next cycle should try composing them; this is a
genuinely additive pair, not the substitutive stack that failed in 0005.
Drop the parallel-array route (v003) — replacing a hash with an O(n)
under-reorder shift is a locality regression. Treat hit-rate as still fully
capped, and probe the put-p99 tail as the one unexplained latency source.

# Cycle 0007 Insight

## Cohort outcome

All three variants forked from the cycle-0006 v001 trivial-hasher side-table
parent and tried to wring more latency from the `target_heat` probe: fuse the
hasher and capacity wins into one (v001), swap the HashMap for a direct-mapped
array (v002), and move the per-put heat-clear to the eviction site (v003). All
three entered the Winners, but the cohort overturned the cycle's framing —
every win landed on a different op than its hypothesis named, and the get
median proved untouchable.

## Patterns

- The composition was free but mis-aimed. Adding capacity pre-reservation on
  top of the trivial hasher (v001) regressed nothing and stayed bit-for-bit on
  hit-rate and metadata, but its tail win surfaced on the **put** path, not the
  get-p99 the disjoint-cause model predicted. The get path was already pinned
  at its hasher floor with no rehash spike left to remove, so the reservation's
  only headroom was the table-growth cost that put-side hits were absorbing.
- get-p50 is now a hard floor. Both v001 and v002 left the get median flat;
  v002's structurally cheaper direct-mapped array — meant to undercut the
  SwissTable group scan — did not move it at all. Cycle 0006's hasher swap had
  already removed the only median-path cost; what remains on the side-table
  probe is tail variance, not median latency.
- The structurally cheaper table still pays off as a variance reducer. v002's
  flat array dropped both p99 tails and put-p50 while holding hit-rate exactly,
  confirming 2×-capacity sizing makes slot collisions a negligible
  promotion-timing perturbation — a safe substitute even though it doesn't
  touch the median.
- The put-p99 tail is owned by eviction/cascade work, not the side-table
  touch. v003 confirmed this negatively: the per-put `remove` was the cheapest
  possible operation (a non-resident negative lookup that short-circuits), and
  relocating it to the eviction path turned it into a real resident remove
  behind new branches, regressing both put metrics.

## Open questions

- With get-p50 pinned and the side-table probe's median cost gone, is any
  get-path median lever left, or is get latency fully converged?
- v003 located the put-p99 tail in the eviction/cascade machinery. Is that
  cascade reachable without disturbing gate decisions or hit-rate, or is it the
  irreducible cost of the demotion structure?

## Continuation

Stop targeting get-p50 — two independent routes this cycle confirmed it is at
a hard hasher floor with no probe-side headroom left. Carry forward v001
(capacity reservation, a free put-tail win) and/or v002 (direct-mapped array,
tighter p99s) as the latency baseline; they are both safe, hit-rate-neutral.
The live frontier is now the **put path**, and v003 pinpointed its p99 bound as
the eviction/cascade work, not the side table — next cycle should probe that
cascade directly rather than economizing on the per-put probe, which is already
the cheapest form of its operation. Treat hit-rate as still fully capped.

# Cycle 0008 Insight

## Cohort outcome

All three variants forked from the cycle-0007 incumbents and attempted
"behavior-preserving" structural moves on the dash segment: reorder the get
lookup branches stash-last (v001), relocate the per-put heat clear to the
demotion site (v002), and collapse the two-tier demotion cascade to a single
stash hop (v003). All three entered the Winners, but none was a clean win —
each move's premise was contradicted by where the work actually lives, and the
cohort overturned two standing assumptions at once.

## Patterns

- The get median lives in the **stash**, not the promoted tiers. v001 assumed
  the hottest hits resolve in target/probing and pay a wasted stash scan, so it
  moved stash last — and get-p50 regressed, because the median get hit actually
  resolves in the stash and now pays two failed scans before reaching it. The
  branch-ordering lever is real but points stash-*first*, the inverse of the
  hypothesis. Behavior was preserved exactly (hit-rate/metadata bit-for-bit);
  only the cost model was inverted.
- Relocating a probe off the median path trades median for tails. v002 did
  shave put-p50 by deleting the unconditional per-put heat clear, confirming
  that touch was real hot-path work — but the clear didn't vanish, it landed on
  the demotion branches and resurfaced as wider put-p99/get-p99 and a worse
  get-p50 summary. Moving work off the median is not free when the destination
  adds branching the tail then exposes — the same lesson cycle 0007's v003 taught
  on the eviction path.
- Hit-rate is **not** perfectly conflict-insensitive. v003 cut the put-p99
  cascade exactly as cycle 0007 predicted by collapsing the foreign-resident
  retry to a single stash hop — but hit-rate slipped below the parent, because
  the one-more-chance re-home was salvaging a small number of hits. This is the
  first crack in the multi-cycle "hit-rate fully capped / conflict-insensitive"
  framing: the demotion cascade is a genuine latency-vs-hit-rate trade, not pure
  overhead.

## Open questions

- If the get median resolves in the stash, is a stash-first reordering an
  actual get-p50 win, or does promoting the stash branch only relocate the cost
  onto the promoted-tier hits the way v002 relocated the put clear?
- The put-p99 cascade is now a priced trade: how large is the hit-rate cost of
  the single-hop demotion, and is there a cheaper conflict-mitigation step that
  keeps most of the rescued hits without the double-hop tail?

## Continuation

Two assumptions this cohort relied on were wrong and should be dropped: hot
get hits do **not** live in the promoted tiers (the median is in the stash, so
try stash-*first* if probing get-p50 at all), and the demotion cascade is **not**
free on hit-rate (collapsing it trades a few hits for the put-p99 win). The
put-p99/hit-rate trade (v003) and the put-p50/tail trade (v002) are both now
characterized as trades, not clean wins — next cycle should decide whether
either trade is worth banking rather than seeking a strictly-free version, and
should treat "hit-rate fully capped" as no longer exact in the conflict/demotion
machinery.

# Cycle 0009 Insight

## Cohort outcome

All three variants forked from cycle-0007 incumbents and worked the demotion
cascade and get-path arithmetic that prior cycles had flagged: gate the
cascade retry on a non-full target (v001), defer the target/probing index math
past the stash branch (v002), and add a second rescue level to the cascade
(v003). All three entered the Winners, but none was clean — two were
characterized trades and one refuted its own premise, and together they
established that cascade depth is a continuous latency↔hit-rate dial coupled
to the get path through the stash.

## Patterns

- The cascade is a bidirectional dial, not a fixed cost. v001 shortened it
  (route full-target items straight to stash) and v003 deepened it (one more
  rescue level); the shallow direction sheds put-p99 and concedes hit-rate,
  the deep direction buys hit-rate and widens put-p99. v003 pushed hit-rate
  above the long-standing 0.6794 cap for the first time — but barely, at a
  steeply diminishing rate where each added level buys far less residency than
  the tail it widens. The cap is breakable but not cheaply.
- The stash is a shared resource that couples put-side cascade work to
  get-side latency. v001 revealed the parent's double-hop `put_at` was not pure
  waste: it kept the stash short at the get path's expense. Diverting
  full-target items into the stash to save the put tail lengthened the chain
  the stash-first get must scan, regressing get-p50/p99. Any cascade economy
  that ends in the stash pays at the get median — the two paths cannot be
  optimized in isolation.
- get-p50 is not arithmetic-bound. v002 deferred two confirmed-wasted
  `get_index` calls off the median stash-resolving path and get-p50 rose, not
  fell — the calls sat below the noise floor and the code motion only
  perturbed codegen. This closes cycle 0008's open question: the median get is
  hasher/probe-bound and fully converged; shaving "wasted" index math is not a
  lever.

## Open questions

- Both cascade directions ended in the stash and paid there. Is there a
  conflict-mitigation step that resolves victims *without* growing stash
  occupancy — so the put-tail win and the get-median cost decouple?
- v003 cleared the 0.6794 cap by a hair at large put-p99 cost. Is there any
  residency above the cap reachable at a tolerable tail, or is the cap
  effectively the practical ceiling given the diminishing return?

## Continuation

Three levers are now closed: get-p50 is hasher-bound (drop index-arithmetic
moves entirely), and both cascade directions are priced trades, not clean
wins. The load-bearing discovery for the next cycle is the **stash coupling** —
put-side cascade work and get-side median latency are linked through stash
occupancy, so any cascade change must be scored on both ops at once, not just
the one it targets. If pursuing hit-rate past 0.6794, expect to pay put-p99
steeply; if pursuing the put tail, expect get-p50 to absorb it via a longer
stash. Next cycle should look for a conflict-resolution path that does *not*
terminate in the stash, since that is the only way seen to break the trade
rather than slide along it.
